source.title: Improving Pretraining Data Using Perplexity Correlations
source.authors: Tristan Thrush; Christopher Potts; Tatsunori Hashimoto

record.tranche_reason: Tests downstream predictability from language-model losses using observational correlations and held-out predictions, rather than the parameter/token/compute scaling measurements in the claim.
record.gate_note: The paper’s pretraining data-selection results report downstream benchmark outcomes after selecting data, but do not test power-law scaling or compute-optimal allocation, so they are not rows for those versions. Results cited from other papers are not recorded as rows.
record.test_reason: Across 90 public LLMs (≈33M–9B), the study predicts held-out benchmark performance from per-domain web-corpus losses and from mean loss. These are its own results on V6's 'predictable from pretraining loss' part, in a new observational cross-model setting. It does not fit scaling laws in parameters, tokens or compute.
record.authors_conclusion: The record's paraphrase over-weights prediction. The main conclusion is that perplexity-benchmark correlations from public models give an effective, training-free pretraining data selector. At 160M it beats DSIR and matches the best DCLM fastText filter. In preregistered runs up to 1.4B its gains grow with scale on the raw pool, with no benefit on the already-filtered pool. As a secondary analysis, losses predict benchmark rankings well, except for models trained on unusual data.
record.recipe_differences: Uses observational loss-to-benchmark correlations and held-out ranking predictions across public models, rather than fitting or testing parameter-, token-, or compute-scaling laws.
record.method_sensitivity: Training data distribution: predictions are weaker for models trained on unusual data.

fits_no_version.finding: Selecting pretraining domains whose loss correlates with a benchmark improved that benchmark in controlled pretraining at 160M. Gains over baselines grew with scale from 160M to 1.4B on the raw DCLM pool, with no benefit on the pre-filtered pool.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Lowering loss on benchmark-correlated domains through data selection causally raises downstream performance, with benefits growing with scale.

record.problems: The text says the 95% bootstrapped confidence intervals are wide enough that no individual comparison is significant. Most prediction scores are shown only in figures, without their numerical values stated in the text. Prediction is weaker for models trained on unusual data.
record.rows_left_out: Pretraining data-selection benchmark outcomes are not rows because they test data selection effects rather than the claim versions about scaling or downstream predictability. Cited scaling-law findings are excluded.

untested.parts: Downstream improvement as a function of parameter count, tokens or compute. The loss used is per-domain web-corpus bits-per-byte across heterogeneous models, not each model's own held-out pretraining loss.

missing.what: Numeric held-out R² per task for the raw estimate, the projected estimate and the mean-loss baseline. These are needed to judge how strong loss-to-benchmark predictability is.

record.verdict_notes: The study is not an original source. The V6 evidence is observational and cross-model, mostly figure-only, and the authors note that mean loss alone is nearly as predictive as their estimator.

versions.untested_parts: Power-law loss scaling in parameter count, tokens, or compute.
Extrapolating power-law loss fits from smaller to much larger runs.
Compute-optimal parameter and token allocation as a function of compute.
How architecture details affect loss at fixed parameter count.
Power-law behavior in other modalities or training regimes.
The study predicts benchmark performance from losses; it does not test downstream improvement as a function of scale.
Whether scaling-law exponents or compute-optimal splits depend on setup, or whether scaling curves bend.

rows.subject: 90 Open LLM Leaderboard LLMs (aggregate)
rows.operation_detail: Five-fold held-out prediction of benchmark performance using the raw correlation estimate
rows.uncertainty: 95% bootstrapped confidence intervals are wide enough that no individual comparison is significant
rows.note: The figure reports the raw correlation estimate, but the text does not give its numerical scores or characterize this estimate separately.
rows.check: The raw-estimate R² values appear only in Figure 6. The 'no individual comparison significant' caveat concerns comparisons between estimators, not whether R² differs from zero.

rows.subject: 90 Open LLM Leaderboard LLMs (aggregate)
rows.operation_detail: Five-fold held-out prediction of benchmark performance using the projected correlation estimate
rows.value: figure only; projected estimate beats the mean-loss baseline on 7 of 8 tasks
rows.uncertainty: 95% bootstrapped confidence intervals; p=0.035 for projected estimate gains over the baseline
rows.note: The paper calls the prediction results strong, while noting that no individual comparison is significant; the stated aggregate comparison favors the projected estimate.
rows.check: The value given, beating mean loss on 7 of 8 tasks (p=0.035), compares the study's own estimator with a baseline; that is a method comparison. Only the held-out R² level itself bears on V6, and it is shown in the figure only (authors call it 'strong').

rows.subject: 90 Open LLM Leaderboard LLMs (aggregate)
rows.operation_detail: Prediction of benchmark performance using mean loss across domains
rows.value: figure only; authors describe average loss as a strong predictor
rows.uncertainty: 95% bootstrapped confidence intervals are wide enough that no individual comparison is significant
rows.note: This is the stated mean-loss prediction baseline; individual numerical R² values are not given in the text.
rows.check: This is the row most directly on V6: mean loss across domains is 'a strong predictor of model performance'. It should be role main, not comparator. R² values are in the figure only.

relationships.condition: 90 Open LLM Leaderboard models on 8 benchmarks (LAMBADA and its translations, ARC Easy, PIQA, SciQ), five-fold held-out prediction from losses, including Mamba and extreme vocabulary, context and parameter sizes
relationships.reason: Mean loss is a strong held-out predictor (R3). Per-domain losses give accurate held-out rank predictions (R2, R4, R5), and these hold for unusual architectures and sizes (R7). Values are figure-only.
relationships.display_finding: Mean loss strongly predicted held-out performance, while per-domain losses accurately predicted rankings even for unusual architectures, vocabularies, context lengths, and parameter sizes.

relationships.condition: Models trained on atypical data (e.g. Phi, multilingual, code, GPT-4-output data)
relationships.reason: The authors state these models are not as well predicted from losses, and Figure 4 shows them outside 2σ (R6).
relationships.display_finding: Models trained on atypical data fell outside 2σ of the predictions and were less accurately predicted from losses.

source_check.scope: Only the listed rows, labels and statements were checked; presence is not whole-study approval.

reader_labels.label: supports
reader_labels.condition: Tested models and benchmarks, including the reported PIQA and French LAMBADA examples
reader_labels.reason: The authors report generally accurate held-out rank predictions and a strong prediction signal from average loss; the projected estimate beats the mean-loss baseline on 7 of 8 tasks (R2–R5).

reader_labels.label: limits_scope
reader_labels.reason: Predictions are worse for models trained on unusual data, so the reported relationship does not generalize equally across training-data distributions (R6).
